claims.text: The proposed intervention combines an ab initio-trained machine-learned interatomic potential with enhanced-sampling free-energy integration.
The ML training data will span both solid and liquid states.
The hybrid method can calculate fusion and high-temperature phase free energies of multicomponent high-entropy alloys with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The hybrid method will reduce computational cost by 10–100× relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed domain includes elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys from approximately 0.8Tm to 1.1Tm.
Both solid and liquid phases are present under the stated near-melting conditions.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations require substantially more computational time and resources.
ML interatomic potentials can approximate an ab initio potential-energy landscape with near-DFT precision in multicomponent refractory alloys.
An MTP for bcc MoNbTaW achieved test-set energy errors of only a few meV per atom.
The accuracy and transferability of the ML potential mediate efficient thermodynamic sampling from the ab initio energy landscape.
Enhanced sampling will properly integrate vibrational entropy and anharmonic contributions to the phase free energies.
Enhanced sampling combined with the ML potential will properly retain electron–vibration coupling.
The hybrid method will reproduce explicit-MD phase free energies within a few meV per atom.
Melting temperatures and derived thermodynamic observables from the hybrid method will deviate only minimally from explicit ab initio MD results.
The hybrid method will outperform TOR-TILD in multicomponent regimes.
The method is expected to work at ambient pressure across elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems near fusion.
Applicability at lower temperatures or in systems with non-standard bonding environments is uncertain.
The hypothesis is falsified if phase-free-energy discrepancies exceed a few meV per atom, melting-temperature errors are correspondingly significant, or speedup is less than one order of magnitude.
